nameStory: The dooryard violet earned its humble name by being the reliable little purple flower that pops up right outside your door each spring. Unlike its woodland cousins that hide in forests, this violet is perfectly content growing in the disturbed soil around homes, gardens, and pathways where people live and work.
description: Dooryard violet is a small, low-growing perennial that forms neat little clumps of heart-shaped leaves and cheerful purple flowers. The entire plant typically stays under 6 inches tall, making it easy to overlook until those distinctive violet blooms catch your eye in early spring. Each plant sends up separate flower stems from a central root system, creating small colonies that spread gradually over time.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Classic violet-shaped flowers with five purple petals, including a distinctive lower petal with purple veining that acts as a landing strip for bees. The flowers have a light, sweet fragrance and feel papery-thin when gently touched.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Heart-shaped leaves with rounded teeth along the edges, growing on individual stems directly from the ground (no main plant stem). The leaves feel smooth and slightly waxy, with prominent veining visible when held up to light.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Forms low clumps with leaves and flowers arising separately from ground level, never forming an upright stem. Plants spread by underground runners to create small colonies.

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: Produces small, three-sided green capsules that split open explosively when ripe, shooting tiny brown seeds several feet away with an audible 'pop' if you listen closely.

habitat: Thrives in the disturbed soils around human habitation - gardens, lawn edges, pathways, and waste areas with partial shade to full sun. Prefers moist, rich soil but tolerates a wide range of conditions including compacted earth. Often found mixed with dandelions, plantain, and other common yard plants.

seasonality.spring: Blooms peak in April and May with those unmistakable purple flowers appearing before many other plants wake up. New heart-shaped leaves emerge bright green and tender.
seasonality.summer: Flowers fade but leaves remain green and expand, though plants may go dormant during hot, dry spells. Look for the exploding seed capsules in mid to late summer.
seasonality.fall: Leaves may produce a second, smaller flush of blooms in cool weather. Foliage begins to yellow and die back as temperatures drop.
seasonality.winter: Plants go completely dormant with no visible above-ground parts. Look for the withered brown remains of last year's leaves to mark where plants will return.

funFact: Dooryard violets are botanical time-travelers - they produce two completely different types of flowers! The showy purple spring blooms everyone notices are often sterile, while the plant secretly makes tiny, closed flowers later in summer that never open but produce most of the seeds.
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with common blue violet, but dooryard violet typically grows in more disturbed, sunny locations rather than woodland settings. The leaves tend to be slightly more pointed at the tip, and the flowers often have more intense purple veining on the lower petal.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called 'dooryard violet,' this species is sometimes lumped together with common blue violet by botanists, and the exact boundaries between violet species can be blurry. What matters for identification is recognizing the classic violet flower shape and growth pattern rather than worrying about precise species names.
compareHints: Among the purple violets in New England, dooryard violet is distinguished by its preference for disturbed, sunny locations rather than deep woods like Canada violet or specialized habitats like marsh blue violet. It's smaller and less robust than common blue violet, with leaves that tend to be more triangular-heart-shaped rather than perfectly rounded.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among New England's many violet species, common blue violet stands out for its fuzzy, truly heart-shaped leaves with rounded tips, unlike the pointed-tip hearts of Canada violet or the deeply lobed leaves of bird's foot violet.

Among New England's yellow violets, Round-leaved Violet is unique for its perfectly circular leaves - Downy Yellow Violet has heart-shaped leaves, and Smooth Yellow Violet has oval leaves that taper to points.

Among New England's many violet species, bird's foot violet is the odd one out with its deeply divided leaves - all other violets have simple, undivided leaves that are heart-shaped, oval, or rounded.
Among New England's yellow violets, smooth yellow violet is distinguished by its completely hairless leaves and stems, while downy yellow violet has soft, fuzzy foliage.
Among New England's many violet species, Canada Violet stands out for its height and white flowers with yellow centers.
Among New England's many violet species, Labrador violet stands out for its purple-tinted foliage - most other violets have plain green leaves.
Among New England's many violet species, long-spurred violet stands out with its exceptionally long nectar spur and preference for deep woods rather than edges or clearings.
Among New England's many violet species, downy blue violet stands out for its consistently fuzzy foliage - most other blue violets like common blue violet and marsh blue violet have smooth leaves.
Among New England's many violets, white bog violet is unique for its combination of white flowers and extremely narrow leaves.
Among New England's many violet species, marsh blue violet stands out for its wet habitat requirements - most other blue violets prefer drier conditions.
Among New England's white violets, northern white violet is distinguished by its wetland habitat preference and more prominent purple veining on flowers.

Among New England's many violet species, arrowleaf violet stands out for its narrow, elongated leaves - most others like common blue violet and Canada violet have distinctly rounded or heart-shaped leaves.
Among New England's white-flowered violets, sweet white violet is distinguished by its low, stemless growth habit and subtle fragrance.

Among New England's yellow violets, the downy yellow violet is distinguished by its fuzzy, soft-haired leaves and stems, plus its unique growth pattern with leaves both at ground level and on upright stems.

Among New England's white violets, kidneyleaf white violet stands out with its unique kidney-shaped leaves - sweet white violet has heart-shaped leaves, northern white violet has narrow lance-shaped leaves, and Canada violet has pointed, toothed leaves.

Among New England's many violet species, European field pansy stands out for its tiny size and pale, cream-colored flowers - most other violets have larger, more distinctly purple, blue, yellow, or white flowers.
Among New England's many violet species, great-spurred violet stands out for its exceptionally long flower spur and notably hairy leaves.
Among New England's many violet species, three-lobed violet stands out for its hand-shaped leaves - most other violets have heart-shaped, round, or lance-shaped leaves that aren't deeply divided.
Among white violets in New England, largeleaf white violet stands out for its substantially larger leaves compared to sweet white violet or northern white violet.
Among New England's many violets, hookedspur violet stands out for its hooked spur - most other blue violets like common blue violet have straight or only slightly curved spurs.
Among New England's white-flowered violets, primrose-leaved violet stands out for its oval leaves that are twice as long as wide with rounded bases.

Among New England's white-flowered violets, cream violet is unique for its purple stripes - Canada violet is pure white and much taller, while sweet white violet is smaller and lacks the striped pattern.
Sweet violet stands out from New England's many native violets primarily by its strong fragrance and European origin.
Among New England violets, wavy-leaved violet is unique in having deeply divided, wavy-edged leaves right from early spring emergence.

Among New England's many violet species, Britton's Coast Violet stands apart with its deeply-divided leaves that look almost fern-like compared to the heart-shaped or rounded leaves of common blue violet or the simple oval leaves of marsh blue violet.
Unlike common blue violet which grows in gardens and lawns, alpine marsh violet is much smaller and restricted to wet mountain habitats.
Among New England's many violets, Northern Woodland Violet is distinguished by its forest habitat preference and relatively small size.
New England Violet is distinguished from other violets primarily by its diminutive size - it's like a miniature version of the common blue violet.
Among New England's many violet species, Wild Pansy stands out for its face-like flower pattern and multiple colors per bloom, while most other violets are solid purple, blue, yellow, or white.
Among New England's many violets, northern bog violet stands out for its distinctive kidney-shaped leaves that are broader than long - most other violets have heart-shaped or lance-shaped leaves.
Among New England violets, Le Conte's violet is distinguished from common blue violet by its more compact size and flowers that don't rise significantly above the leaves.
Unlike most native New England violets, common dog-violet has a very short, blunt spur and spreads aggressively by runners rather than staying in neat clumps.
Among New England's many violet species, southern wood violet stands out for its consistently fuzzy texture throughout the plant.
Among New England violets, pectinate-leaved violet is unmistakable due to its comb-like divided leaves - no other violet in the region has leaves cut into such narrow segments.
Unlike common blue violet or sweet white violet which have relatively short, normal-sized sepals, the Long Sepal Violet's sepals extend dramatically beyond the petals.
Unlike the more familiar common blue violet with its heart-shaped leaves and solid purple flowers, American field pansy has much smaller, multi-colored pansy-like blooms and narrower leaves.
